content:
Shoulder osteoarthritis causes a deep, aching pain in the shoulder, stiffness and grinding, and difficulty reaching up or behind your back. It is less common than knee or hip osteoarthritis and is often linked to age, past injury or long-standing rotator cuff problems. Most people are helped by exercise, pain relief and activity changes. Joint replacement is an option if symptoms are severe.

The two shoulder joints

The shoulder has two joints that can be affected:

  • the glenohumeral joint, the main ball-and-socket joint. Arthritis here causes deep pain and stiffness.
  • the acromioclavicular (AC) joint at the top of the shoulder. Arthritis here causes pain at the top of the shoulder, particularly when reaching across your body.

Symptoms

  • aching pain deep in the shoulder, sometimes spreading down the upper arm
  • stiffness and reduced movement, especially turning the arm outwards or reaching up
  • grinding or clicking
  • pain at night, particularly lying on the affected side
  • difficulty with tasks such as hair washing, dressing or reaching high shelves

Conditions that can look similar

  • frozen shoulder: severe stiffness, often with intense pain, usually in people aged 40 to 60 and more common with diabetes
  • rotator cuff problems: pain when lifting the arm out to the side, weakness and pain at night
  • referred pain from the neck: pain that moves down the arm with neck movement
  • polymyalgia rheumatica: stiffness in both shoulders and hips, mainly in over 50s, with severe morning stiffness
  • rheumatoid arthritis, which can affect both shoulders

A GP or physiotherapist can usually tell these apart through examination. An X-ray may be used to confirm shoulder osteoarthritis and plan treatment.

Self-care

  • keep the shoulder moving gently every day to prevent further stiffness
  • pace overhead tasks and keep items you use often at waist to shoulder height
  • heat from a wheat bag can ease stiffness. Cold packs can help after activity.
  • sleep with a pillow supporting the arm, or lie on the other side
  • pain relief: ask your pharmacist about painkillers and anti-inflammatory gels that suit you

Exercises

A physiotherapist can give you a programme. Common exercises include:

  • pendulum swings: lean forward and let the arm hang, then make small circles
  • wall slides: walk your fingers up a wall, in front and to the side
  • assisted movements with a stick, using the good arm to help the sore one
  • strengthening with a resistance band for the rotator cuff and shoulder blade muscles

Some discomfort is normal. If pain is much worse the next day, do a little less.

NHS treatment options

  • physiotherapy: many areas let you self-refer
  • steroid injections: can reduce pain for some weeks to months, helping you do your exercises
  • surgery: for severe pain or loss of function despite other treatments. Options include shoulder replacement, either anatomical or reverse replacement depending on your rotator cuff. For AC joint arthritis, a small operation to remove the end of the collarbone may be offered.

NICE recommends exercise and education for osteoarthritis and referral for joint surgery when symptoms substantially affect quality of life.

Daily life tips

  • use a long-handled brush and sponge for washing
  • choose front-fastening clothes and put the sore arm in first
  • use a step stool rather than reaching up, if your balance is good
  • carry shopping close to your body and split it into lighter bags

Driving and work

If your shoulder limits steering or checking blind spots, you may need to adapt or stop driving until it improves. Tell your employer if work involves reaching or lifting; reasonable adjustments may help.

Outlook

Shoulder osteoarthritis tends to change slowly, and symptoms often go through better and worse spells. Keeping the shoulder moving and the surrounding muscles strong gives you the best chance of staying independent with everyday tasks.

When to get urgent help

Call 999 or go to A&E if you have:

  • a joint that suddenly becomes hot, red, swollen and very painful, especially if you feel feverish or unwell (this can be a joint infection)
  • chest pain, sudden breathlessness, or signs of a stroke such as face drooping, arm weakness or slurred speech

Contact NHS 111 or your GP the same day if symptoms are getting worse quickly, you cannot put weight on a leg, or you are worried and not sure where to go. If you are under a rheumatology team, use their advice line for flares and medicine questions.
